e.etymology: A surname from an Anglo-Norman form of burg, a fortified place. It became one of the great family names of Ireland through the Norman de Burgh family.
A pet form of Emmanuel and its Spanish form Manuel, from Hebrew Immanuel, God is with us. It has also served as a short form of Manfred.
namesakes: Manny Pacquiao (boxing champion from the Philippines)

assoc.t: Manny the woolly mammoth in the Ice Age films
Manny Delgado on Modern Family
Handy Manny, Disney Junior repairman
manny, informal word for a male nanny

e.etymology: A vintage American pet name in the style of Mollie, Sallie and Hallie, most used around 1900. It served as a short form of names beginning with Mal-, such as Malinda.
Hawaiian ka, the, and lena, yellow, a color once associated with royalty in Hawaii. It was later also used as the Hawaiian rendering of Karen.
The form of Abdullah used in Somalia, northern Nigeria and elsewhere in Africa, from Arabic abd Allah, servant of God. Abdullah was the name of the Prophet Muhammad's father.
A Yiddish name from gut or git, good, with the affectionate ending -el. It is a traditional name among Ashkenazi Jews and remains common in Hasidic communities.
A respelling of Kennedy, the Irish surname O Cinneide, from a byname made of ceann, head, and a second word read as helmeted or misshapen. Its use as a first name honors the Kennedy family.

assoc.t: President John F. Kennedy and his family, by sound

e.etymology: A respelling of Jensen, the Danish surname meaning son of Jens, the Danish form of John. The -syn spelling follows Emersyn and Carsyn and is given mostly to girls.
In Yiddish, Liba is a traditional name from lib, dear or beloved, and is the usual source in the US. In Czech it is a short form of Libuse, from a Slavic root that also means dear.
A respelling of Maverick, a word for an independent person that comes from Samuel Maverick, a Texas rancher of the 1800s who left his cattle unbranded.

assoc.t: Maverick, Tom Cruise's pilot in Top Gun, by sound
Dallas Mavericks NBA team, by sound
Ford Maverick pickup truck, by sound

e.etymology: From Mailen, a name of the Mapuche people of Chile and Argentina, related to the Mapudungun word malen, girl or young woman. It is widely used in Argentina.
From Arabic fatih, conqueror or opener, and fath, victory. In Punjabi fateh means victory, and the name is common among Sikhs, recalling Fateh Singh, the youngest son of Guru Gobind Singh.
Built on Norman, north man, with a feminine -i ending. Its use follows the singer Normani, who rose to fame in the group Fifth Harmony in the 2010s.

assoc.t: Normani, pop and R&B singer from Fifth Harmony

e.etymology: The French form of Latin Paulina, a feminine form of Paul, from paulus, small or humble. It has been in regular English use since the 1800s and peaked in the US around 1910.
namesakes: Pauline Kael (film critic for The New Yorker)

assoc.t: Pauline, the woman Mario rescues in Donkey Kong
The Perils of Pauline, classic cliffhanger film serial

e.etymology: A short form of Germanic names containing hild, battle, in use since the Middle Ages. Saint Hilda of Whitby was a 7th-century English abbess, and Hildr is a valkyrie in Norse myth.
namesakes: Saint Hilda of Whitby (7th-century English abbess)

assoc.t: Aunt Hilda on Sabrina the Teenage Witch
Hilda, blue-haired heroine of the Netflix cartoon

e.etymology: A spelling of Jessie, the pet form of Jessica, and of the boys' name Jesse, from Hebrew Yishai, the father of King David. In the US it is given to both girls and boys.
A Spanish-language spelling of Janet, the medieval pet form of Jane. Jane is a feminine form of John, from Hebrew Yochanan, God is gracious.
The Italian form of Dominic, from Late Latin Dominicus, belonging to the Lord. It was traditionally given to boys born on Sunday and honors Saint Dominic, founder of the Dominican order.
A spelling of Kiara, an English-language respelling of the Italian Chiara, from Latin clarus, bright or clear. Kiara is also sometimes linked to the Irish name Ciara.

assoc.t: Kiara, Simba's daughter in The Lion King II, by sound

e.etymology: A surname from a medieval pet form of Patrick, Latin Patricius, nobleman. As a first name it calls up General George S. Patton, the American commander of World War II.

assoc.t: General George S. Patton of World War II
Patton, 1970 best picture winner starring George C. Scott

e.etymology: From the Old English name Eadric, joining ead, wealth or fortune, and ric, ruler. It was borne by Anglo-Saxon nobles, including Eadric the Wild, who resisted the Norman Conquest.
The Russian form of Elijah, from Hebrew Eliyahu, my God is Yahweh, which reached Russian through Byzantine Greek. Ilya Muromets is the great hero of Russian folk epics.

assoc.t: Ilya Rozanov, hockey star in the series Heated Rivalry

e.etymology: A modern American name in the Josiah family that puts Jah, a short Biblical form of God's name, up front. Josiah is Hebrew for the Lord supports.
A modern American name that joins Kenzie, from the Scottish surname Mackenzie, with the -leigh ending; a spelling of Kensley. It has no meaning apart from its parts.
A double-L spelling of Elora, a name that spread after the baby Elora Danan in the 1988 film Willow. It also matches Ellora, the site of famous rock-cut cave temples in western India.

assoc.t: Ellora Caves, ancient rock-cut temples in India

e.etymology: In Bulgarian, Zahari is the form of Zachary, from Hebrew Zekharyah, the Lord has remembered. In the US it also follows the sound of Zahara, Jahari and Amari and is given to girls and boys alike.

e.meaning: from Courtenay, a place in France
e.etymology: A K spelling of Courtney, from the aristocratic Norman surname Courtenay. The surname comes from a place in France named for a Roman called Curtenus, from Latin curtus, short.

assoc.t: Kourtney Kardashian, reality TV star

e.etymology: A spelling of Jacey or Jaycee, which grew out of the initials J.C. and as a pet form of Jacqueline. It spread in the 1990s and 2000s in step with Macie, Kacie and Lacie.
A spelling of Jayden, coined by American parents at the end of the 20th century by joining the initial J to the sound of Aidan, Braden and Hayden. It has no meaning of its own.
From the English name of the lark, a small bird known for singing in flight at dawn. It is also an English surname that began as a nickname or for a catcher of larks.
namesakes: Lark Voorhies (Lisa Turtle on Saved by the Bell)

assoc.t: lark, the songbird
a lark, something done just for fun

e.etymology: An older spelling of Annie, the pet form of Ann and Anna, from Hebrew Hannah, grace or favor. The spelling is also used in German and the Scandinavian languages.
The Dutch form of Henry, from a Germanic name joining haim, home, and rik, ruler. Its relatives include German Heinrich, French Henri and Scandinavian Henrik.
